0.title: The Letter of Jude: Contend for the Faith
0.overview:
Jude is one of the most neglected letters in the New Testament. Most Christians know the doxology at the end — and it is magnificent — but could not tell you what comes before it. What comes before it is some of the most urgent, vivid, and pastorally charged writing in the entire canon. Jude is a fire-bell.

The author identifies himself as “a servant of Jesus Christ and brother of James” (v. 1). He does not say “brother of the Lord” — though he almost certainly was. Matthew 13:55 and Mark 6:3 name “Judas” among the brothers of Jesus, and James was the recognized head of the Jerusalem church. Jude had credentials that would have opened every door in the early Christian world: raised in the same household as the Son of God, converted after the resurrection, brother to the most respected Jewish-Christian leader of the first generation. He uses none of it. He calls himself a servant of Jesus Christ. The biological relationship, once the most important fact about him, has been swallowed up by a greater reality: the resurrection has changed the category. He no longer has a brother who happens to be the Messiah; he has a Lord who happens to have been his brother.

The occasion for the letter is stated plainly in v. 3. Jude had intended to write about “our common salvation” — a warm, constructive letter celebrating the faith they shared. He never wrote it. The crisis was too pressing. False teachers had “crept in unnoticed” (v. 4), and Jude found himself writing an alarm instead of a celebration. The letter we have is not the letter he planned. This matters pastorally: faithful ministry sometimes means setting aside what we intended to say in order to say what the moment requires.

How is Jude related to 2 Peter 2, which says many of the same things? Most scholars think 2 Peter used Jude; some think Jude used 2 Peter, or that both drew on common teaching. The more likely reading is that Peter knew Jude’s letter and adapted it. That takes nothing from either: an inspired writer may use another’s words, as the prophets and apostles often did.

The letter is twenty-five verses. It has no chapter breaks. It is a single sustained argument that moves from the alarm (vv. 3–4), through the evidence (vv. 5–16), to the counter-strategy for the faithful (vv. 17–23), and finally to one of the greatest doxologies in Scripture (vv. 24–25). The fire and the doxology belong together. The letter that begins with danger ends with adoration — and the adoration is not escapism. It is the theological ground on which the whole letter stands. You can contend for the faith without bitterness, rescue others without losing yourself, hold on under pressure — because the One who keeps you is infinitely more powerful than everything that threatens you.

1.title: Contend, Hold Fast, Adore
1.overview:
Jude’s one chapter moves in four steps. He states why he writes: contend for the faith, because false teachers have slipped in (vv. 3–4). He gives the evidence: three examples of judgment on people who had privilege and despised it (vv. 5–7), then a vivid portrait of the false teachers who are repeating the pattern (vv. 8–16). He turns to the faithful: remember, build up, pray, keep yourselves in God’s love and rescue the wavering (vv. 17–23). And he ends with God, who is able to keep his people from stumbling (vv. 24–25).

The order matters. The darkness of vv. 5–16 is framed by the people who are “called, beloved… and kept” (v. 1) and the God “who is able to keep you” (v. 24). Jude warns in order to make his readers brave, not anxious: the courage of people who know they are held.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Before any warning, Jude tells the church who they are: called (God summoned them), beloved in God the Father (they rest in his love now) and kept for Jesus Christ (guarded until he comes). Every alarm that follows is heard by people God is holding.
verseByVerse.theology:
Called, Beloved, Kept

Before any warning, Jude tells the church who they are: called, beloved in God the Father, kept for Jesus Christ. The warnings are heard by people God is holding.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: A church shaken by false teachers is first reminded of its security.

Now: A believer who fears drifting away begins where Jude begins: not with their grip on God, but with his grip on them.

verseByVerse.quote: Jude, a servant of Jesus Christ and brother of James, To those who are called, beloved in God the Father and kept for Jesus Christ: May mercy, peace, and love be multiplied to you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jude, a servant of Jesus Christ and brother of James, To those who are called, beloved in God the Father and kept for Jesus Christ: May mercy, peace, and love be multiplied to you.

Meaning first. Jude is a short, urgent letter calling believers to contend for the faith against ungodly intruders. Jude greets those who are called, loved by God and kept for Jesus Christ (vv. 1–2). He had intended to write about their shared salvation, but had to urge them instead to fight for the faith delivered once for all to the saints, because ungodly people had slipped in who turn God’s grace into a licence for immorality and deny Jesus Christ (vv. 3–4). He reminds them of God’s past judgements: Israel in the wilderness, the angels who abandoned their position, and Sodom and Gomorrah (vv. 5–7). The intruders defile the flesh, reject authority and slander heavenly beings, where even the archangel Michael left judgement to the Lord; they follow Cain, Balaam and Korah, and are like hidden reefs, waterless clouds, dead trees, wild waves and wandering stars (vv. 8–13). Enoch prophesied their judgement when the Lord comes with his holy ones; they are grumblers, boasters and flatterers (vv. 14–16). The apostles foretold such scoffers, who divide and are devoid of the Spirit (vv. 17–19). But believers must build themselves up in the faith, pray in the Spirit, keep themselves in God’s love, wait for Christ’s mercy, and show mercy to the doubting and the endangered (vv. 20–23). The letter ends with one of the greatest doxologies in Scripture: to him who is able to keep you from stumbling and present you blameless before his glory with great joy be glory forever (vv. 24–25).

Setting and background. Jude (Judas) was a brother of James and of Jesus, who, like James, did not believe in Jesus during his ministry (John 7:5) but came to faith after the resurrection (Acts 1:14). He is named among Jesus’ brothers in Mark 6:3. The date is uncertain, perhaps AD 60–80. His readers are unknown, probably Jewish Christians, given his use of Old Testament and Jewish examples. Much of the letter closely parallels 2 Peter 2.

Jude, a servant of Jesus Christ. Key words. “Servant” (doulos, slave). Like James (James 1:1), Jude does not call himself Jesus’ brother, but his slave. Humility; and the recognition that the relationship that matters is not physical family but faith.

And brother of James. Key words. James, the well-known leader of the Jerusalem church. Identifying himself through James gives his letter weight.

To those who are called. Key words. “Called” (klētois): God’s effectual call (Romans 8:28–30).

Beloved in God the Father. Key words. “Beloved” (ēgapēmenois, perfect tense: having been loved and remaining loved). God’s love, set on them in eternity, continues.

And kept for Jesus Christ. Key words. “Kept” (tetērēmenois, perfect tense: guarded and still guarded). Kept by God for Christ, until his return, as a treasure is kept for its owner. Three great truths frame the letter: called, loved, kept. And it ends with the God who is able to keep (v. 24). Amid all the warnings, believers are secure.

May mercy, peace, and love be multiplied to you. Key words. “Multiplied” (plēthyntheiē, increased, abundant).

What it does not mean. “Kept” does not mean believers are passive. Jude will command them to keep themselves (v. 21). God keeps them, and they keep themselves, both together.

In a sentence. From Jude, a servant of Jesus Christ and a brother of James, to those who have been called, who are loved in God the Father and kept for Jesus Christ: mercy, peace and love be yours in abundance.

For worship. Thank God that you are called, loved and kept. Nothing in this letter’s warnings can undo that.
verseByVerse.note: Jude (Judas) was a brother of James and of Jesus, who, like James, came to faith after the resurrection. Much of his letter is closely paralleled in 2 Peter 2.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jude meant to write a warm letter about “our common salvation”, but the danger forced him to write an alarm instead. The result is one of the key sentences in the New Testament on how the church relates to its doctrine: “contend for the faith that was once for all delivered to the saints.” The faith is given, complete, and must be guarded.
verseByVerse.theology:
Contend for the Faith

The faith was delivered once for all to the saints. False teachers turn grace into sensuality and deny the only Master and Lord, Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Jude set aside the letter he wanted to write because the danger was urgent.

Now: Contend as someone who loves the people being misled, not as someone who enjoys a fight.

verseByVerse.quote: Beloved, although I was very eager to write to you about our common salvation, I found it necessary to write appealing to you to contend for the faith that was once for all delivered to the saints. For certain people have crept in unnoticed who long ago were designated for this condemnation, ungodly people, who pervert the grace of our God into sensuality and deny our only Master and Lord, Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Beloved, although I was very eager to write to you about our common salvation, I found it necessary to write appealing to you to contend for the faith that was once for all delivered to the saints. For certain people have crept in unnoticed who long ago were designated for this condemnation, ungodly people, who pervert the grace of our God into sensuality and deny our only Master and Lord, Jesus Christ.

Beloved, although I was very eager to write to you about our common salvation. Key words. “Very eager” (pasan spoudēn poioumenos, making every effort). “Common salvation” (koinēs sōtērias, shared salvation): the salvation all believers have in common. Jude had planned a positive letter about it.

I found it necessary to write appealing to you to contend for the faith. Key words. “Necessary” (anankēn, compulsion). Circumstances forced a change of plan. “Contend” (epagōnizesthai, fight earnestly, struggle hard, as an athlete strains in a contest). “The faith” (tē pistei): not personal trust here, but the body of truth believed, the gospel.

That was once for all delivered to the saints. Key words. “Once for all” (hapax): a single, final, complete delivery. “Delivered” (paradotheisē, handed down, entrusted as a tradition). The faith was given by God through the apostles, complete and unchangeable. Nothing can be added to it or subtracted from it. This is the basis of the closed canon and sola Scriptura: the apostolic faith, recorded in Scripture, is final.

For certain people have crept in unnoticed. Key words. “Crept in unnoticed” (pareisedysan, slipped in sideways, sneaked in). Like spies infiltrating a camp. They were inside the church.

Who long ago were designated for this condemnation. Key words. “Long ago” (palai). “Designated” (progegrammenoi, written beforehand, marked out in advance). Either their condemnation was written beforehand in Scripture (the examples that follow), or God had appointed it in advance. Their judgement is not a surprise to God.

Ungodly people. Key words. “Ungodly” (asebeis, irreverent, without regard for God). A key word of Jude (vv. 4, 15, 18).

Who pervert the grace of our God into sensuality. Key words. “Pervert” (metatithentes, change, alter, turn into). “Sensuality” (aselgeian, unrestrained immorality). They twisted grace into a licence to sin: since we are forgiven, sin does not matter (Romans 6:1–2). Antinomianism.

And deny our only Master and Lord, Jesus Christ. Key words. “Master” (despotēn, sovereign) and “Lord” (kyrion). They denied his lordship by their lives and perhaps by their teaching (2 Peter 2:1; Titus 1:16). Grammatically, “only Master and Lord” both refer to Jesus Christ, a strong statement of his deity.

Where Christians differ: is the faith still developing through new revelation? Some churches hold that doctrine develops through ongoing revelation or the church’s teaching office, adding new dogmas over time; some charismatics expect new prophetic revelation. Verdict: Jude says the faith was delivered “once for all.” The apostolic deposit is complete. The church’s understanding of Scripture may deepen, but no new doctrine may be added. Scripture alone is the final rule of faith, and the canon is closed.

What it does not mean. “Contend” does not mean being quarrelsome or harsh. It means standing firm for the truth, earnestly and lovingly (v. 22; 2 Timothy 2:24–25).

In a sentence. Dear friends, although I was very eager to write to you about the salvation we share, I felt compelled to write and urge you to contend for the faith that was once for all entrusted to God’s holy people. For certain individuals whose condemnation was written about long ago have secretly slipped in among you. They are ungodly people, who pervert the grace of our God into a licence for immorality and deny Jesus Christ, our only Sovereign and Lord.

On a Tuesday. Learn the faith well enough to contend for it. Is there a teaching that turns grace into permission to sin? Stand against it.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Three examples make one point: privilege does not protect from judgment. Israel was redeemed from Egypt; the angels stood in God’s presence; Sodom had righteous Lot in its midst. Each had unusual exposure to God, each turned from him, and each was judged. The false teachers are repeating the pattern.
verseByVerse.theology:
Privilege Is No Shield

Israel redeemed from Egypt, angels who left their place, and Sodom and Gomorrah all show that privilege does not exempt anyone from judgement.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The false teachers belonged to the church but were walking Israel’s, the angels’ and Sodom’s road.

Now: The person most at risk is not the one who has never heard, but the one who has heard so often that the gospel has become background noise.

verseByVerse.quote: Now I want to remind you, although you once fully knew it, that Jesus, who saved a people out of the land of Egypt, afterward destroyed those who did not believe. And the angels who did not stay within their own position of authority, but left their proper dwelling, he has kept in eternal chains under gloomy darkness until the judgment of the great day — just as Sodom and Gomorrah and the surrounding cities, which likewise indulged in sexual immorality and pursued unnatural desire, serve as an example by undergoing a punishment of eternal fire.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now I want to remind you, although you once fully knew it, that Jesus, who saved a people out of the land of Egypt, afterward destroyed those who did not believe. And the angels who did not stay within their own position of authority, but left their proper dwelling, he has kept in eternal chains under gloomy darkness until the judgment of the great day — just as Sodom and Gomorrah and the surrounding cities, which likewise indulged in sexual immorality and pursued unnatural desire, serve as an example by undergoing a punishment of eternal fire.

Now I want to remind you, although you once fully knew it. Key words. “Once” (hapax, once for all). They knew these truths; they needed reminding (2 Peter 1:12).

That Jesus, who saved a people out of the land of Egypt. Key words. Some manuscripts read “the Lord,” others “Jesus,” others “God.” “Jesus” has strong early support and is probably original (the harder reading). If so, Jude attributes the exodus to the pre-existent Christ, as Paul does (1 Corinthians 10:4, 9). A striking statement of Christ’s eternal deity.

Afterward destroyed those who did not believe. Key words. “Afterward” (to deuteron, the second time). The generation redeemed from Egypt died in the wilderness for unbelief (Numbers 14; Hebrews 3:16–19). Being part of God’s people outwardly does not guarantee salvation.

And the angels who did not stay within their own position of authority. Key words. “Position of authority” (archēn, rule, domain, rank). The second example. Angels who abandoned their God-given place. Jewish tradition (1 Enoch) connected this with the “sons of God” and the daughters of men (Genesis 6:1–4), as in 2 Peter 2:4.

But left their proper dwelling. Key words. “Proper dwelling” (oikētērion, home, habitation): heaven.

He has kept in eternal chains under gloomy darkness until the judgment of the great day. Key words. A wordplay: they did not keep (tērēsantas) their position, so God keeps (tetērēken) them in chains. “Eternal chains” (desmois aidiois). “Great day”: the final judgement.

Just as Sodom and Gomorrah and the surrounding cities. Key words. The third example. Admah and Zeboiim (Deuteronomy 29:23).

Which likewise indulged in sexual immorality and pursued unnatural desire. Key words. “Likewise”: like the angels, they crossed boundaries God set. “Indulged in sexual immorality” (ekporneusasai, gave themselves over to immorality). “Unnatural desire” (sarkos heteras, other flesh, different flesh). The men of Sodom sought sexual relations with the visitors (Genesis 19:4–5), who were angels, and their sin included same-sex intercourse. The phrase may emphasise both: pursuing flesh of a different kind (angels, unknowingly), and desire contrary to God’s design.

Serve as an example by undergoing a punishment of eternal fire. Key words. “Example” (deigma, sample, specimen). “Eternal fire” (pyros aiōniou). The fire that destroyed the cities is a picture of the eternal fire of final judgement (Matthew 25:41).

Where Christians differ: is punishment eternal, or do the wicked cease to exist? Annihilationists hold that the wicked are destroyed and cease to exist; universalists that all are eventually saved. Verdict: Jude speaks of “eternal chains” and “eternal fire” (vv. 6–7) and “utter darkness reserved forever” (v. 13). Jesus used the same word, eternal, for both punishment and life (Matthew 25:46). Scripture teaches conscious, eternal punishment for those who reject God (Revelation 14:11; 20:10). This truth is held with sorrow and with urgency to warn and to rescue (v. 23).

What it does not mean. It does not mean those who struggle with same-sex attraction are beyond grace. All sinners may be washed and forgiven (1 Corinthians 6:9–11). It means sexual immorality of every kind is serious before God.

In a sentence. Though you already know all this, I want to remind you that Jesus, who delivered his people out of Egypt, later destroyed those who did not believe. And the angels who did not keep their positions of authority but abandoned their proper dwelling, he has kept in darkness, bound with everlasting chains for judgement on the great Day. In a similar way, Sodom and Gomorrah and the surrounding towns gave themselves up to sexual immorality and perversion. They serve as an example of those who suffer the punishment of eternal fire.

For worship. Thank God that in Christ you are rescued from the judgement you deserved. Pray for those still under it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–13 — The False Teachers: A Portrait
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jude now paints the false teachers in image after image: they defile, reject authority and mock what they do not understand; they walk the road of Cain, Balaam and Korah; they are reefs, clouds without rain, dead trees, foaming waves and wandering stars. Each image describes people who promise nourishment and give nothing, or worse.
verseByVerse.theology:
A Portrait of False Teachers

Even Michael would not pronounce judgement on the devil but said, “The Lord rebuke you.” These men blaspheme what they do not understand, and walk in the way of Cain, Balaam and Korah.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: They shared the church’s love feasts while feeding only themselves.

Now: Beware teaching that looks impressive and spiritual but leaves people no closer to Christ and no more holy.

verseByVerse.quote: Yet in like manner these people also, relying on their dreams, defile the flesh, reject authority, and blaspheme the glorious ones. But when the archangel Michael, contending with the devil, was disputing about the body of Moses, he did not presume to pronounce a blasphemous judgment, but said, “The Lord rebuke you.” But these people blaspheme all that they do not understand, and they are destroyed by all that they, like unreasoning animals, understand instinctively. Woe to them! For they walked in the way of Cain and abandoned themselves for the sake of gain to Balaam’s error and perished in Korah’s rebellion. These are hidden reefs at your love feasts, as they feast with you without fear, shepherds feeding themselves; waterless clouds, swept along by winds; fruitless trees in late autumn, twice dead, uprooted; wild waves of the sea, casting up the foam of their own shame; wandering stars, for whom the gloom of utter darkness has been reserved forever.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Yet in like manner these people also, relying on their dreams, defile the flesh, reject authority, and blaspheme the glorious ones. But when the archangel Michael, contending with the devil, was disputing about the body of Moses, he did not presume to pronounce a blasphemous judgment, but said, “The Lord rebuke you.” But these people blaspheme all that they do not understand, and they are destroyed by all that they, like unreasoning animals, understand instinctively. Woe to them! For they walked in the way of Cain and abandoned themselves for the sake of gain to Balaam’s error and perished in Korah’s rebellion. These are hidden reefs at your love feasts, as they feast with you without fear, shepherds feeding themselves; waterless clouds, swept along by winds; fruitless trees in late autumn, twice dead, uprooted; wild waves of the sea, casting up the foam of their own shame; wandering stars, for whom the gloom of utter darkness has been reserved forever.

Yet in like manner these people also, relying on their dreams. Key words. “Relying on their dreams” (enypniazomenoi, dreaming): claiming visions and revelations as authority for their teaching and conduct. False prophecy based on dreams (Jeremiah 23:25–32). They put private experience above the faith delivered.

Defile the flesh, reject authority, and blaspheme the glorious ones. Key words. Three charges, matching the three examples: immorality (Sodom), rebellion (Israel), and contempt for spiritual beings (angels). “Glorious ones” (doxas): angelic beings, as in 2 Peter 2:10.

But when the archangel Michael, contending with the devil, was disputing about the body of Moses. Key words. The dispute over Moses’ body is not in the Old Testament; it comes from a Jewish tradition, perhaps recorded in a lost work called the Assumption of Moses. God buried Moses (Deuteronomy 34:5–6), and the tradition said the devil claimed his body. Michael is the archangel (Daniel 10:13, 21; 12:1; Revelation 12:7).

He did not presume to pronounce a blasphemous judgment, but said, The Lord rebuke you. Key words. Michael, mighty as he was, left judgement to God (compare Zechariah 3:2). He did not insult Satan in his own authority.

But these people blaspheme all that they do not understand. Key words. Arrogance born of ignorance.

And they are destroyed by all that they, like unreasoning animals, understand instinctively. Key words. What they do understand, their animal instincts and appetites, is what destroys them (2 Peter 2:12).

Woe to them! For they walked in the way of Cain. Key words. Three examples of rebellious men. Cain: envy, hatred, murder, rejecting God’s way of approach (Genesis 4; 1 John 3:12).

And abandoned themselves for the sake of gain to Balaam’s error. Key words. Balaam: greed, leading God’s people into immorality and idolatry for money (Numbers 22–25; 31:16; 2 Peter 2:15).

And perished in Korah’s rebellion. Key words. Korah: rebellion against God’s appointed leaders, Moses and Aaron, for which the earth swallowed him (Numbers 16). “Perished” (past tense): their fate is as good as sealed.

These are hidden reefs at your love feasts. Key words. Five vivid pictures from nature. “Hidden reefs” (spilades, rocks hidden below the water, on which ships are wrecked; or “stains,” spots). “Love feasts” (agapais): the fellowship meals of the early church, often with the Lord’s Supper. The false teachers were present, hidden dangers.

As they feast with you without fear, shepherds feeding themselves. Key words. “Without fear” (aphobōs, without reverence). Shepherds feeding themselves (Ezekiel 34:2, 8): leaders who care only for themselves.

Waterless clouds, swept along by winds. Key words. Clouds that promise rain but give none (Proverbs 25:14).

Fruitless trees in late autumn, twice dead, uprooted. Key words. Trees that should be bearing fruit at harvest but have none (Matthew 7:17–19). “Twice dead”: dead in fruitlessness and dead with roots torn up; perhaps spiritually dead and destined for the second death (Revelation 20:14).

Wild waves of the sea, casting up the foam of their own shame. Key words. Restless, raging, leaving filthy foam and debris on the beach (Isaiah 57:20).

Wandering stars, for whom the gloom of utter darkness has been reserved forever. Key words. “Wandering stars” (asteres planētai, planets, or shooting stars, or perhaps fallen angels in Jewish imagery). Unreliable for navigation, leading sailors astray. Their destiny: eternal darkness.

Textual note. Jude draws on Jewish traditions that are not in the Old Testament, here and in verses 14–15. Quoting or alluding to a writing does not make that writing Scripture; Paul quoted pagan poets (Acts 17:28; Titus 1:12). Jude’s inspired use affirms the truth of the particular point he cites.

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers should fear demons or be preoccupied with angels. It means they should not be arrogant about spiritual matters, and should leave judgement to God.

In a sentence. In the very same way, on the strength of their dreams these ungodly people pollute their own bodies, reject authority and heap abuse on celestial beings. But even the archangel Michael, when he was disputing with the devil about the body of Moses, did not himself dare to condemn him for slander but said, “The Lord rebuke you!” Yet these people slander whatever they do not understand, and the very things they do understand by instinct, as irrational animals do, will destroy them. Woe to them! They have taken the way of Cain; they have rushed for profit into Balaam’s error; they have been destroyed in Korah’s rebellion. These people are hidden reefs at your love feasts, eating with you without the slightest qualm, shepherds who feed only themselves. They are clouds without rain, blown along by the wind; autumn trees, without fruit and uprooted, twice dead. They are wild waves of the sea, foaming up their shame; wandering stars, for whom blackest darkness has been reserved for ever.

On a Tuesday. Test teachers by their fruit: are they serving the flock or themselves? Are they giving water or just promising it?
verseByVerse.note: The dispute over Moses’ body is not in the Old Testament; it was known from Jewish tradition. Cain, Balaam and Korah stand for murderous hatred, greed and rebellion.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jude quotes a prophecy found in 1 Enoch, a Jewish book widely read in his day: the Lord is coming with countless holy ones to judge the ungodly for their deeds and their words. He says Enoch “prophesied”; he does not say the book is Scripture. Its message matches the rest of the Bible (Daniel 7:10; Matthew 25:31).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Prophecy of Enoch

Jude cites a true prophecy from 1 Enoch without calling the book Scripture: the Lord will come with his holy ones to judge the ungodly for their deeds and their words.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The false teachers grumbled, boasted and flattered people for gain.

Now: A true shepherd says what people need to hear; a false one says what pays.

verseByVerse.quote: It was also about these that Enoch, the seventh from Adam, prophesied, saying, 'Behold, the Lord comes with ten thousands of his holy ones, to execute judgment on all and to convict all the ungodly of all their deeds of ungodliness that they have committed in such an ungodly way, and of all the harsh things that ungodly sinners have spoken against him.' These are grumblers, malcontents, following their own sinful desires; they are loud-mouthed boasters, showing favoritism to gain advantage.
verseByVerse.commentary:
It was also about these that Enoch, the seventh from Adam, prophesied, saying, ‘Behold, the Lord comes with ten thousands of his holy ones, to execute judgment on all and to convict all the ungodly of all their deeds of ungodliness that they have committed in such an ungodly way, and of all the harsh things that ungodly sinners have spoken against him.’ These are grumblers, malcontents, following their own sinful desires; they are loud-mouthed boasters, showing favoritism to gain advantage.

It was also about these that Enoch, the seventh from Adam, prophesied. Key words. Enoch, who walked with God and was taken (Genesis 5:18–24; Hebrews 11:5). “Seventh from Adam”: counting Adam as the first (Adam, Seth, Enosh, Kenan, Mahalalel, Jared, Enoch). Jude quotes 1 Enoch, a Jewish writing well known at the time (1 Enoch 1:9). Jude does not call 1 Enoch Scripture, but affirms that this particular prophecy is true, perhaps preserved by tradition from Enoch himself.

Behold, the Lord comes with ten thousands of his holy ones. Key words. “Comes” (ēlthen, came, a prophetic past: as certain as if already done). “Ten thousands” (myriasin, myriads). “Holy ones”: angels (Deuteronomy 33:2; Zechariah 14:5; Matthew 25:31; 2 Thessalonians 1:7).

To execute judgment on all and to convict all the ungodly. Key words. “Convict” (elenxai, expose, prove guilty). “Ungodly” appears four times in one sentence: their whole character is ungodliness.

And of all the harsh things that ungodly sinners have spoken against him. Key words. “Harsh things” (sklērōn, hard, defiant words). God judges words as well as deeds (Matthew 12:36–37).

These are grumblers, malcontents. Key words. “Grumblers” (gongystai, murmurers), like Israel in the wilderness (1 Corinthians 10:10). “Malcontents” (mempsimoiroi, complainers about their lot, blamers of fate).

Following their own sinful desires. Key words. Ruled by desire.

They are loud-mouthed boasters. Key words. “Loud-mouthed” (hyperonka, swelling, bombastic), as in 2 Peter 2:18.

Showing favoritism to gain advantage. Key words. “Showing favoritism” (thaumazontes prosōpa, admiring faces, flattering). They flatter the influential for profit (James 2:1–9).

Where Christians differ: does quoting 1 Enoch make it Scripture? The Ethiopian Orthodox Church includes 1 Enoch in its canon. Verdict: Jude quotes one prophecy from 1 Enoch and affirms it as true, as Paul quoted true statements from pagan poets. This does not make the whole book inspired. The church, including Jesus and the apostles, did not recognise 1 Enoch as part of the Hebrew Scriptures, and it contains much that is legendary. The canon is closed and does not include it.

What it does not mean. It does not mean grumbling is a minor sin. Scripture treats it as rebellion against God’s providence.

In a sentence. Enoch, the seventh from Adam, prophesied about them: ‘See, the Lord is coming with thousands upon thousands of his holy ones to judge everyone, and to convict all of them of all the ungodly acts they have committed in their ungodliness, and of all the defiant words ungodly sinners have spoken against him.’ These people are grumblers and faultfinders; they follow their own evil desires; they boast about themselves and flatter others for their own advantage.

On a Tuesday. Watch for grumbling in your own heart this week. Replace it with thanks.
verseByVerse.note: Jude quotes 1 Enoch, a Jewish writing well known at the time. Quoting it does not make it Scripture; Paul also quoted pagan poets.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–23 — Hold Fast: The Call to the Faithful
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: “But you, beloved.” Jude turns from the false teachers to the people he loves. The apostles foretold such scoffers, so their arrival is no reason to panic. Then he gives the faithful their task: build yourselves up, pray in the Spirit, keep yourselves in God’s love, wait for Christ’s mercy, and rescue those in danger, each in the way they need.
verseByVerse.theology:
But You, Beloved

Build yourselves up in the faith, pray in the Holy Spirit, keep yourselves in God’s love, and wait for Christ’s mercy. Then show mercy to the wavering and snatch others from the fire.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The apostles had foretold scoffers in the last time.

Now: Meet each person where they are: patience for the doubting, urgency for the endangered, and care for yourself in the rescue.

verseByVerse.quote: But you must remember, beloved, the predictions of the apostles of our Lord Jesus Christ. They said to you, 'In the last time there will be scoffers, following their own ungodly passions.' It is these who cause divisions, worldly people, devoid of the Spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But you must remember, beloved, the predictions of the apostles of our Lord Jesus Christ. They said to you, ‘In the last time there will be scoffers, following their own ungodly passions.’ It is these who cause divisions, worldly people, devoid of the Spirit.

But you must remember, beloved, the predictions of the apostles of our Lord Jesus Christ. Key words. “Remember” (mnēsthēte). “Predictions” (rhēmatōn, words spoken beforehand). The apostles warned of this (Acts 20:29–30; 1 Timothy 4:1; 2 Timothy 3:1–5; 2 Peter 3:3). Jude seems to speak of the apostles as a past generation.

They said to you, In the last time there will be scoffers, following their own ungodly passions. Key words. “Last time”: the whole period since Christ’s coming. “Scoffers” (empaiktai, mockers), as in 2 Peter 3:3.

It is these who cause divisions. Key words. “Cause divisions” (apodiorizontes, make separations, draw boundaries). Perhaps claiming to be a spiritual elite, dividing the church into first- and second-class Christians.

Worldly people. Key words. “Worldly” (psychikoi, natural, soulish, unspiritual), as in 1 Corinthians 2:14 and James 3:15. Living by natural human nature, not by the Spirit. Ironic, if they claimed superior spirituality.

Devoid of the Spirit. Key words. “Devoid of the Spirit” (pneuma mē echontes, not having the Spirit). The decisive mark: they are not Christians at all (Romans 8:9).

What it does not mean. It does not mean every division in the church is caused by unbelievers. But those who divide the church by claiming a higher spirituality while living for the flesh show they lack the Spirit.

In a sentence. But, dear friends, remember what the apostles of our Lord Jesus Christ foretold. They said to you, ‘In the last times there will be scoffers who will follow their own ungodly desires.’ These are the people who divide you, who follow mere natural instincts and do not have the Spirit.

For worship. Thank God for the apostles’ warnings, and for the Spirit who lives in you.

verseByVerse.quote: But you, beloved, building yourselves up in your most holy faith and praying in the Holy Spirit, keep yourselves in the love of God, waiting for the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ that leads to eternal life. And have mercy on those who doubt; save others by snatching them out of the fire; to others show mercy with fear, hating even the garment stained by the flesh.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But you, beloved, building yourselves up in your most holy faith and praying in the Holy Spirit, keep yourselves in the love of God, waiting for the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ that leads to eternal life. And have mercy on those who doubt; save others by snatching them out of the fire; to others show mercy with fear, hating even the garment stained by the flesh.

But you, beloved. Key words. “But you”: in contrast with the scoffers. Now Jude gives the positive instructions.

Building yourselves up in your most holy faith. Key words. “Building up” (epoikodomountes, building on a foundation). “Most holy faith”: the apostolic faith (v. 3), holy because it comes from God. Build your life on it, growing in knowledge of Scripture and sound doctrine (Colossians 2:7; Acts 20:32).

And praying in the Holy Spirit. Key words. “Praying in the Holy Spirit” (en pneumati hagiō proseuchomenoi): prayer guided, empowered and inspired by the Spirit, according to God’s will (Romans 8:26–27; Ephesians 6:18). The Spirit whom the scoffers lack (v. 19) helps believers pray.

Keep yourselves in the love of God. Key words. The main command. “Keep” (tērēsate, guard, preserve), echoing verse 1 (“kept for Jesus Christ”) and verse 6. God keeps them; they keep themselves in his love. Remain where God’s love can be enjoyed, by obedience and fellowship (John 15:9–10).

Waiting for the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ that leads to eternal life. Key words. “Waiting” (prosdechomenoi, eagerly expecting). “Mercy”: the mercy Christ will show at his return, bringing believers into the fullness of eternal life. Note the Trinity: Holy Spirit, God (the Father), Lord Jesus Christ.

And have mercy on those who doubt. Key words. Three groups needing different responses. “Those who doubt” (diakrinomenous, waver, are unsettled): believers shaken by the false teachers. Show them patient, compassionate help.

Save others by snatching them out of the fire. Key words. “Snatching” (harpazontes, seizing, grabbing quickly). Those already deeply influenced, on the edge of destruction, need urgent rescue (Amos 4:11; Zechariah 3:2).

To others show mercy with fear, hating even the garment stained by the flesh. Key words. Those most deeply corrupted. Still show mercy, but with caution (“fear”), lest you be dragged down too (Galatians 6:1). “Garment stained” (spilōmenon chitōna, soiled undergarment): an image of moral pollution (Zechariah 3:3–4). Love the sinner, hate the sin, and beware its contamination.

Textual note. The manuscripts differ in verses 22–23, some describing two groups, others three. The ESV follows the three-group reading, which has good early support.

Where Christians differ: does “praying in the Holy Spirit” mean praying in tongues? Some charismatic believers take it as speaking in tongues. Verdict: Nothing in the context mentions tongues. Praying in the Spirit means praying under the Spirit’s guidance and in dependence on him, according to God’s will revealed in his word (Ephesians 6:18). All believers can and should pray this way.

What it does not mean. “Keep yourselves” does not mean salvation depends on our own power to keep ourselves. God keeps us (vv. 1, 24); we actively keep ourselves by the means he provides.

In a sentence. But you, dear friends, by building yourselves up in your most holy faith and praying in the Holy Spirit, keep yourselves in God’s love as you wait for the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ to bring you to eternal life. Be merciful to those who doubt; save others by snatching them from the fire; to others show mercy, mixed with fear, hating even the clothing stained by corrupted flesh.

On a Tuesday. Is someone you know wavering in their faith? Reach out to them with mercy this week.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The letter that began with alarm ends in adoration. After so many examples of those who stumbled, Jude lifts our eyes to the God who is able to keep his people from stumbling and present them blameless with great joy. The doxology is not an add-on. It is the ground on which the whole letter stands.
verseByVerse.theology:
Him Who Is Able

The letter full of stumbling ends with the God who is able to keep his people from stumbling and present them blameless before his glory with great joy.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: A church under pressure was pointed to God’s glory, majesty, dominion and authority.

Now: The same God holds his people through every crisis, and will bring them home.

verseByVerse.quote: Now to him who is able to keep you from stumbling and to present you blameless before the presence of his glory with great joy, to the only God, our Savior, through Jesus Christ our Lord, be glory, majesty, dominion, and authority, before all time and now and forever. Amen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now to him who is able to keep you from stumbling and to present you blameless before the presence of his glory with great joy, to the only God, our Savior, through Jesus Christ our Lord, be glory, majesty, dominion, and authority, before all time and now and forever. Amen.

Now to him who is able to keep you from stumbling. Key words. “Able” (dynamenō, has the power). “Keep” (phylaxai, guard, protect, as a sentry). “From stumbling” (aptaistous, without falling, sure-footed, like a horse that does not stumble). After all the warnings, the final word is God’s power to keep his people. The letter begins with believers “kept for Jesus Christ” (v. 1) and ends with God “able to keep.” Perseverance rests on God.

And to present you blameless before the presence of his glory with great joy. Key words. “Present” (stēsai, cause to stand). “Blameless” (amōmous, without blemish, like a perfect sacrifice; Ephesians 5:27; Colossians 1:22). “His glory”: God’s glorious presence. “Great joy” (agalliasei, exultation): God’s joy and ours, as the bride is presented to the bridegroom.

To the only God, our Savior, through Jesus Christ our Lord. Key words. “Only God”: there is one God. “Our Savior” (1 Timothy 1:1). “Through Jesus Christ”: all glory to God comes through Christ the mediator.

Be glory, majesty, dominion, and authority. Key words. Four words of praise. “Glory” (doxa, splendour). “Majesty” (megalōsynē, greatness). “Dominion” (kratos, power, might). “Authority” (exousia, right to rule).

Before all time and now and forever. Amen. Key words. Past, present, future. God’s glory is eternal. “Amen”: so be it.

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers never sin. It means God will keep them from falling away and bring them faultless, cleansed by Christ’s blood, into his presence.

In a sentence. To him who is able to keep you from stumbling and to present you before his glorious presence without fault and with great joy, to the only God our Saviour, be glory, majesty, power and authority, through Jesus Christ our Lord, before all ages, now and for evermore! Amen.

For worship. Pray or sing this doxology aloud today. He is able to keep you, and one day he will present you blameless with great joy.

1.text: <sup>1</sup>Jude, a servant of Jesus Christ and brother of James, To those who are called, beloved in God the Father and kept for Jesus Christ:<sup>2</sup>May mercy, peace, and love be multiplied to you.<sup>3</sup>Beloved, although I was very eager to write to you about our common salvation, I found it necessary to write appealing to you to contend for the faith that was once for all delivered to the saints.<sup>4</sup>For certain people have crept in unnoticed who long ago were designated for this condemnation, ungodly people, who pervert the grace of our God into sensuality and deny our only Master and Lord, Jesus Christ.<sup>5</sup>Now I want to remind you, although you once fully knew it, that Jesus, who saved a people out of the land of Egypt, afterward destroyed those who did not believe.<sup>6</sup>And the angels who did not stay within their own position of authority, but left their proper dwelling, he has kept in eternal chains under gloomy darkness until the judgment of the great day—<sup>7</sup>just as Sodom and Gomorrah and the surrounding cities, which likewise indulged in sexual immorality and pursued unnatural desire, serve as an example by undergoing a punishment of eternal fire.<sup>8</sup>Yet in like manner these people also, relying on their dreams, defile the flesh, reject authority, and blaspheme the glorious ones.<sup>9</sup>But when the archangel Michael, contending with the devil, was disputing about the body of Moses, he did not presume to pronounce a blasphemous judgment, but said, “The Lord rebuke you.”<sup>10</sup>But these people blaspheme all that they do not understand, and they are destroyed by all that they, like unreasoning animals, understand instinctively.<sup>11</sup>Woe to them! For they walked in the way of Cain and abandoned themselves for the sake of gain to Balaam’s error and perished in Korah’s rebellion.<sup>12</sup>These are hidden reefs at your love feasts, as they feast with you without fear, shepherds feeding themselves; waterless clouds, swept along by winds; fruitless trees in late autumn, twice dead, uprooted;<sup>13</sup>wild waves of the sea, casting up the foam of their own shame; wandering stars, for whom the gloom of utter darkness has been reserved forever.<sup>14</sup>It was also about these that Enoch, the seventh from Adam, prophesied, saying, “Behold, the Lord comes with ten thousands of his holy ones,<sup>15</sup>to execute judgment on all and to convict all the ungodly of all their deeds of ungodliness that they have committed in such an ungodly way, and of all the harsh things that ungodly sinners have spoken against him.”<sup>16</sup>These are grumblers, malcontents, following their own sinful desires; they are loud-mouthed boasters, showing favoritism to gain advantage.<sup>17</sup>But you must remember, beloved, the predictions of the apostles of our Lord Jesus Christ.<sup>18</sup>They said to you, “In the last time there will be scoffers, following their own ungodly passions.”<sup>19</sup>It is these who cause divisions, worldly people, devoid of the Spirit.<sup>20</sup>But you, beloved, building yourselves up in your most holy faith and praying in the Holy Spirit,<sup>21</sup>keep yourselves in the love of God, waiting for the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ that leads to eternal life.<sup>22</sup>And have mercy on those who doubt;<sup>23</sup>save others by snatching them out of the fire; to others show mercy with fear, hating even the garment stained by the flesh.<sup>24</sup>Now to him who is able to keep you from stumbling and to present you blameless before the presence of his glory with great joy,<sup>25</sup>to the only God, our Savior, through Jesus Christ our Lord, be glory, majesty, dominion, and authority, before all time and now and forever. Amen.
